displayName: Cloud Run Job failure — backtest-screen / backtest-sweep / data-backfill

conditions.displayName: A Cloud Run Job execution logged an error

conditionMatchedLog.filter: resource.type="cloud_run_job" AND resource.labels.job_name=("backtest-screen" OR "backtest-sweep" OR "data-backfill") AND severity>=ERROR

conditions.displayName: A Cloud Run Job task exited non-zero (platform entry; may carry severity DEFAULT)

conditionMatchedLog.filter: resource.type="cloud_run_job" AND resource.labels.job_name=("backtest-screen" OR "backtest-sweep" OR "data-backfill") AND (textPayload:"Task failed" OR textPayload:"failed with" OR jsonPayload.message:"Task failed")

documentation.content:
A Cloud Run **Job** failed. Until FC-096 Phase A nothing in this project watched Jobs at all — all eleven live alert policies match `cloud_run_revision`, i.e. the three services — so a Job that failed, or stopped being executed, was invisible.

Why that matters more for Jobs than for services: **Cloud Scheduler's `jobs:run` is asynchronous.** It records success when the API call returns, not when the execution finishes. A scheduler firing at a Job that fails every time, or at a Job that no longer exists, looks perfectly healthy in the scheduler's own history. This policy is one of the two controls that see through that; the other is the `/regression` `lake_freshness` check, which catches the case where the scheduler is paused or deleted and so never fires at all.

The three Jobs it watches:

- **`backtest-screen`** — the monthly universe screen (`monthly-performance-review`, 1st at 06:00 ET). Its failure means no `backtest_runs` row for the month.
- **`backtest-sweep`** — dashboard-submitted scenario sweeps. A failure here is usually visible to the submitter as a `failed` row in `scenario_sweeps`; the exception is a container killed before it could write one, which is exactly what this catches.
- **`data-backfill`** — the weekly chain/bars backfill (`backfill-weekly`, Saturdays 08:00 ET). Its failure is the quiet one: nothing downstream fails immediately, the lake just stops getting fresher, and the first symptom would be a sweep silently materialising cold months later.

**Two conditions, deliberately.** The first matches anything the Job logs at ERROR — including the Jobs' own structured failure events (`backfill_symbol_failed`, `backfill_unfinished`, `sweep_materialise_failed`, `sweep_store_unavailable`). The second matches the platform's own task-failure entry, because **Cloud Run gives plain-text log lines severity DEFAULT** (the FC-030 lesson: a policy filtering on `severity>=WARNING` alone matched nothing for weeks), so a container that dies without logging JSON would slip past a severity-only filter.

The second condition's text patterns are written against the platform message as documented rather than as observed here. **On the first real failure, confirm the actual entry** and tighten the pattern if it did not match:

```
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_job" AND resource.labels.job_name="data-backfill"' \
  --limit=50 --format='value(severity,textPayload,jsonPayload.event_type)'
```

Triage:

```
gcloud run jobs executions list --job=data-backfill --region=us-central1 --limit=5
gcloud run jobs executions describe <EXECUTION> --region=us-central1
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_job" AND labels."run.googleapis.com/execution_name"="<EXECUTION>"' --limit=100
```

For `data-backfill` specifically, the per-symbol `backfill_symbol_complete` log lines are the record of what a half-finished run actually wrote — a killed execution leaves no terminal summary, and the Job is idempotent, so the remedy is almost always "execute it again with the same window".

Note the exit-code contract: `--command backfill` exits non-zero when **any** symbol did not complete cleanly, and a genuine corporate action (a stock split inside the window) counts as a symbol not completing. That is intended — an operator should hear about a split once — so a legitimate split will page here for roughly the four weekly runs it takes to age out of the trailing window.
